query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the spray nozzle–to–substrate distance in the HVOF process for FeCoNiCrAl bond coats will enhance deposition efficiency and yield thicker coatings while maintaining the in‐flight protection from oxidation, compared to the standard setup using 15–45 μm feedstock.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy powder (15–45 μm) as used in standard HVOF depositions that yield a bond coat below the required thickness.
generation.intervention: Moderately decrease the nozzle-to-substrate (spray) distance during HVOF deposition.
generation.conditions: Thermal spray (HVOF) deposition under controlled inert/low-oxygen conditions at operational parameters that avoid substrate overheating, within the normal fuel/oxygen settings for the alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Higher in-flight particle kinetic energy and reduced flight-time exposure to oxygen lead to better particle impingement and lower oxidation, resulting in a denser, thicker, and well-bonded lamellar structure.
generation.mechanism: A reduced standoff distance shortens the flight path so that particles retain higher kinetic energy upon impact and spend less time in an oxidizing environment. This promotes more efficient splat formation and deposition build-up while limiting the degree of in-flight oxidation that can degrade coating integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The bond coat thickness will increase beyond the baseline achieved with the standard distance and remain dense with preserved microstructural integrity and minimal additional oxide content.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced using a standard spray distance with 15–45 μm feedstock, which show a thickness shortfall despite acceptable coating integrity and low as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.boundary: This intervention should remain effective as long as the reduced distance does not induce excessive substrate heating or cause anomalously high oxide formation due to turbulence; it is limited to HVOF processes with similar material and spray gas compositions.
generation.uncertainty: The proposal builds on evidence that (1) increased spray distance leads to greater in-flight oxidation and reduced thickness (PMC10820071, sections on spraying distance effects) and (2) process parameter adjustments can refine splat formation and deposition efficiency. New to this hypothesis is applying a modest reduction in standoff distance specifically for FeCoNiCrAl bond coats to overcome thickness shortfalls while still mitigating oxidation—quantitative optimization remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of HVOF depositions of the FeCoNiCrAl powder on identical substrates while systematically reducing the nozzle-to-substrate distance (e.g., using several distances below the standard value) and keeping all other parameters constant. After deposition, measure coating thickness, microstructural integrity (via SEM), phase composition/oxidation (via XRD and EDS), and adhesion strength.
measurements: Oxide content and phase identification via XRD
SEM imaging of splat formation and porosity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If reducing the spray distance does not yield a statistically significant increase in coating thickness relative to the standard process—or if the reduction leads to excessive oxidation, microcracking, or lower adhesion compared to the baseline—the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). It is known [] that when Al concentration in FeCoNiCrAlMo0.5 is lower than 10%, FCC solid solution becomes preferable to BCC.
